analysis.one_liner: Restores dealership contracts voided when federally bailed-out automakers went bankrupt.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or a floor vote in the House and died when the Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: After the 2009 taxpayer-funded bailouts, General Motors and Chrysler went through bankruptcy and shut down thousands of dealerships as part of their court-approved restructuring. This bill would have made any automaker the federal government partly owned put those dealership franchise agreements back in place and stripped of nothing — dealers would have kept the legal rights they had before the bankruptcy, including the right to sue under state law. It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee and never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote.
analysis.who_benefits: The direct beneficiaries would have been the roughly 2,000 GM and Chrysler dealers slated for termination in the 2009 bankruptcies — mostly locally owned family businesses and their employees — who would have gotten their franchise agreements back and kept their rights to sue under state law. Communities that depended on dealership jobs and tax revenue would also have benefited.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Locally owned auto dealerships and their employees

how_it_helps.text: It barred any automaker the federal government partly owned from stripping dealers of rights they held before the automaker's bankruptcy, including their rights to sue under state law.
It required those automakers to put the pre-bankruptcy franchise agreements back in place, which would have undone the dealer terminations carried out in the GM and Chrysler restructurings.

analysis.who_pays: GM and Chrysler would have borne the cost of carrying a larger, more expensive dealer network, and because the government owned large stakes in both companies, any added cost would ultimately have touched taxpayers as part-owners. The restructurings were designed to make the automakers leaner; restoring the franchises would have undone part of that.
analysis.who_pays_short: GM and Chrysler, and taxpayers as part-owners

drawbacks.text: The bill would have retroactively overridden court-approved bankruptcy plans for GM and Chrysler, whose dealer cuts were a central part of the restructuring meant to make the companies viable again after the taxpayer-funded bailout.

By forcing the government-owned automakers to carry a larger, costlier dealer network, it could have raised their operating costs and worked against the recovery of companies in which taxpayers held an ownership stake.
It covered only manufacturers in which the federal government had an ownership interest, so it protected some dealers while leaving dealers cut by other companies without recourse.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit would have been real for roughly 2,000 closing dealerships and their employees, who lost businesses built over decades through no fault of their own. The cost is that the terminations were the court-approved core of a rescue designed to make GM and Chrysler small enough to survive; forcing the franchises back could have raised those companies' costs while taxpayers owned large stakes, potentially undercutting the bailout's goal. The bill also offered nothing to dealers cut by manufacturers the government did not own, limiting it to a political window. An honest reading is that the bill protected a specific constituency at the risk of a broader rescue, and it never received the debate that tradeoff deserved.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it expired when the Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: H.R. 2750 was introduced on June 8, 2009 and referred to the House Committee on Financial Services the same day.
The action history shows no further steps: no hearing, no markup, no vote in committee, and no vote on the House floor.
The bill attracted 15 cosponsors, 14 Republicans and 1 Democrat.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: GM and Chrysler came out ahead: the court-approved dealer terminations stood, giving them the leaner dealer networks their restructurings were built around. The committee that never took up the bill also avoided a fight over rewriting those bankruptcy terms.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: GM and Chrysler, whose dealer cuts stood

for.name: Rep. Dennis Kucinich
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor, the only Democrat on the bill at introduction.

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, bringing total support to 15 cosponsors — 14 Republicans and 1 Democrat.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote — leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

against.name: Obama administration auto task force
against.role: Oversaw the GM and Chrysler restructurings
against.what_they_did: Directed the bankruptcy restructurings that closed roughly 2,000 GM and Chrysler dealerships, the terminations this bill would have reversed.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's 15 cosponsors were 14 Republicans and just 1 Democrat (Kucinich of Ohio), though it targeted automakers the Democratic administration had bailed out; no votes were ever taken to reveal a fuller partisan split.

industries.note: The bill would have restored franchise contracts and state-law rights for dealers terminated in the GM and Chrysler bankruptcies, keeping family-owned dealerships open and preserving local jobs. It died without a vote, so the terminations stood.

The restructurings cut the dealer network to lower costs, and this bill would have forced the manufacturers to restore those agreements while taxpayers held ownership stakes. Their interest in a leaner network ran directly against the dealers and communities losing stores.
